title: Elsewhere and Later, a Definition of Learning
author: David Didau
summary: Didau sets out a working definition of learning in three parts, durable, flexible and liminal, and then follows the consequences for what teachers can actually observe. Opening with Cervantes, he notes that learning is something attained rather than performed, so a student can look industrious without learning and look confused while learning a great deal. The central implication is that learning cannot be seen in the present, because retention and transfer are only detectable elsewhere and later, and he offers the image of dark matter, something whose gravitational pull reveals its existence while remaining invisible. From that he derives the learning and performance distinction, arguing that performance during instruction is not merely a weak signal but often positively misleading, since teacher cues and student mimicry inflate what a lesson appears to demonstrate. He then introduces storage strength and retrieval strength to explain the Monday to Friday forgetting that teachers misread as knowledge disappearing, and makes the pointed claim that most classroom activity props up retrieval strength rather than building storage. Desirable difficulties follow as the remedy, with the careful qualifications that they must be a calibrated sequence supported by feedback and must end in success, since overwhelming difficulty stops being desirable. He also states the paradox squarely, that retrieving while retrieval strength is still high degrades storage, so forgetting is a precondition rather than an enemy. The final third fills in liminality with three worked examples, metaphor becoming a way of thinking, simultaneous equations recognized unprompted weeks later, and Versailles reshaping a student's grasp of causation and significance.
points: The three questions he proposes as a teaching test are practical rather than rhetorical: will students know this next year, can they apply it in a new subject or place, and how does it transform their understanding.
Didau's strongest claim is not that in-lesson performance is a weak proxy but that it is often positively misleading, because the conditions producing fluency now can leave little behind.
Storage and retrieval strength give him a diagnosis for Monday-to-Friday forgetting: the knowledge did not vanish, its retrieval strength dropped.
He qualifies desirable difficulty carefully, insisting it is a calibrated sequence with feedback that must still end in success, since overwhelming difficulty ceases to be desirable.
The counterintuitive mechanism is stated plainly: retrieving something while its retrieval strength is high actively degrades storage strength, making forgetting a precondition for durable learning.
quotes: Cervantes makes learning sound wonderfully unpleasant. More interestingly, though, he treats it as something attained rather than something performed. You can look industrious, attentive and scholarly without necessarily having learned anything at all.
The only way to see if something has been retained over time and transferred to a new context is to look at what students can do elsewhere and later.

Learning is like dark matter; it exerts a sort of gravitational pull that reveals its existence but it takes place inside students’ minds. All we can see is what a student is able to do at this moment in time.

Performance during instruction is often positively misleading. Conditions that make students appear successful now can leave surprisingly little behind, while conditions that produce more errors and hesitation seem to lead to better retention later.
Retrieval strength predicts whether we can recall something here and now; storage strength whether we can recall it elsewhere and later.
The bulk of classroom activities are oriented to improving performance rather than learning; propping up retrieval strength instead of bolstering storage.

Not only does retrieving something after it’s become less accessible strengthen subsequent memory, but repeatedly retrieving something while its retrieval strength is high actively degrades storage strength. Paradoxically, forgetting before successful retrieval results in better learning.
But perhaps we’ve merely engineered the conditions in which successful performance is easy.

Once learning has crossed the threshold, it becomes difficult to remember what it was like not to know. Reading, manipulating numbers, recognising irony or understanding why seasons occur come to seem obvious.
